title: Connect to the local API
description: Discover the service and keep authentication private.

sections.title: Use the running address
sections.text: The address shown in Overview belongs to this running instance. Desktop services choose available loopback ports; do not assume a development port. Keep the application running while your client is connected. After restart, discover the new address from the private service.json in that product’s data directory, then verify authenticated /api/v1/capabilities before using it.

sections.title: Two services, two tokens
sections.text: Browser owns profiles. Workbench owns automation and schedules. Each product keeps its own admin-token in its private data directory. CLI users can retrieve the appropriate token with vesper-browser token or vesper-workbench token. The desktop supplies tokens privately to its own views. An external browser opened on documentation receives no token. Set VESPER_TOKEN privately in your script environment; do not paste credentials into URLs, screenshots, source control or shared examples.

sections.title: Check your connection
sections.text: The following read-only example prints this instance’s product, application version and API capabilities. Replace the token placeholder locally. Browser and Workbench expose the same versioned discovery path.

sections.title: What this reference contains
sections.text: The endpoint list comes from the bundled OpenAPI contract. Request fields and any declared response schemas are shown alongside each operation. Some operations declare generic responses; the reference labels these limits rather than inventing a schema. Examples are templates and never run automatically. Versioned API paths are preferred; legacy /api aliases remain available. Documentation is public, read-only contract material on the same local service; API operations retain authentication and origin checks.

title: Profiles, revisions and ownership
description: Edit stopped profiles without racing a running automation.

sections.title: Profile lifecycle
sections.text: Create through POST /api/v1/profiles with settings such as name, engine and locale. Use GET /profiles to reconcile the list, then POST /profiles/{id}/start and /stop. Settings edits require a stopped profile. Duplicate creates independent state. Trash is reversible and does not delete profile bytes. Browser and Workbench share this Browser-owned store through the authenticated service.

sections.title: Revision checks
sections.text: GET /profiles/{id} returns an ETag containing its current revision. Send that exact value as If-Match when PATCHing to avoid overwriting a newer edit. A stale edit returns HTTP 412. Re-read, inspect the change and decide whether to submit a revised update. Avoid blindly retrying edits.

sections.title: Durable run leases
sections.text: POST /profiles/{id}/lease with a runId acquires an automation lease. Creation can use X-Vesper-Run-Id to acquire ownership immediately. Protected operations require X-Vesper-Lease with the returned key. Leases do not silently expire. Stop the owned profile and DELETE /profiles/{id}/lease with the matching key when finished. Explicit administrator interruption stops the browser before revoking ownership; use it only after inspecting an abandoned run.

sections.title: Recoverable admission
sections.text: Use a unique Idempotency-Key for profile creation or supported bulk admissions. Repeating the identical completed request with the same key replays its result. Reusing a key for different input conflicts. An uncertain interrupted operation must be reconciled rather than replayed blindly. Event journal gaps return resetRequired: perform a fresh authenticated list before processing later events.

title: Native identity settings
description: Use qualified policies and understand their limits.

sections.title: Select a qualified native kernel
sections.text: The vesper engine uses a separately qualified native Chromium runtime. Stage, qualify and activate engines through Browser engines while profiles are stopped and automation ownership is released. Operators use packaged kernels; the Chromium source checkout is a developer build requirement. Keep upstream notices and never substitute an unqualified binary under an existing qualification record.

sections.title: Hardware presets and privacy controls
sections.text: The native and desktop-4/desktop-8 identity presets retain the kernel’s browser version, operating system, screen and GPU. Desktop presets pair native CPU and memory policies. Custom enables bounded individual overrides. Fingerprint webgl restricted hides debug vendor/renderer exposure; audio seeded changes completed offline audio deterministically; fonts restricted limits bounded installed font discovery. These settings require runtime proof from the selected kernel.

sections.title: Qualification boundaries
sections.text: These are measured privacy controls, not full arbitrary device personas. They do not qualify complete WebGPU identities, realtime/device audio, all font/media exposure, physical GPU behavior on every machine or browser-wide leak avoidance. Linux software rendering qualification is distinct from physical GPU testing. Unsupported settings must be rejected rather than silently applied through page scripts.

title: Proxy connections
description: Store credentials locally and inspect routing failures.

sections.title: Saved Browser connections
sections.text: Browser /api/v1/proxies stores HTTP or SOCKS5 connections in a local encrypted vault. Public inventory exposes metadata and hasCredentials, never passwords. A profile can copy a saved connection at an explicit revision through savedProxy, or use an inline proxy. Saved references and credentials are omitted from public manifests and exported archives. Re-enter the intended proxy after importing a profile.

sections.title: Workbench inventory
sections.text: Workbench /api/v1/proxies describes its automation inventory. POST /proxies/{id}/check performs a bounded health probe on an unleased item. The Browser proxy manager and Workbench admission inventory have different contracts; do not assume IDs or tokens are interchangeable.

sections.title: Operational limits
sections.text: A successful health check proves the observed probe only. Owned HTTP navigation and outage cases have been tested; whole-browser DNS, UDP, WebRTC, IPv6 and HTTPS outage matrices remain broader acceptance work. Inspect stopped and retained runs before retrying after an uncertain connection failure. Never publish proxy lists, credentials or private test destinations.

title: Archives and extensions
description: Transport profile state and verify the saved result.

sections.title: Profile transport
sections.text: Browser GET /api/v1/profiles/{id}/archive streams a profile archive to a client. The profile must be stopped and lease rules still apply. POST /profiles/import accepts application/gzip with a 512 MiB streaming limit. Imported profiles get an independent identity and proxy credentials are cleared. Archive transfer does not guarantee encrypted cookies will decrypt on a different PC.

sections.title: Workbench saved artifacts
sections.text: A run is saved only after the browser is stopped and the archive is verified. GET /api/v1/runs/{id}/artifact downloads the saved file. Inspect run state and artifact size/hash metadata before treating it as durable output. A retained run or failed export is not a saved run. Resolve cleanup and ownership before retry-export; never discard an original profile while export is uncertain.

sections.title: Manifest V3 extensions
sections.text: Browser /extensions/import accepts application/zip, up to 40 MiB compressed and 128 MiB expanded. Catalog IDs identify immutable versions. Assign a version to a stopped profile after reviewing its permissions. Assigned profiles, including trash, block catalog removal. Profile copies keep their extension packages and storage. Untrusted extensions run with their declared browser permissions.

sections.title: Binary requests
sections.text: Send archive or extension bytes with the exact documented content type; do not wrap them in JSON. JSON request examples do not apply to binary endpoints. Keep profile archives private: cookies, browser history and website storage may contain sensitive data.

sections.title: Restore a saved run in the manager
sections.text: Open Runs & archives and select a saved run. Download its archive and retain the recorded SHA-256 and byte size. In Browser Profiles, use Import and select that .tgz file. Import creates an independent profile with a new ID; it does not overwrite the original. Open the imported profile, inspect the expected owned website state, then stop it normally. Proxy credentials are omitted from transport and must be assigned again. Same-machine cookie recovery is tested separately from cross-PC cookie portability; keep the original profile until you have verified the restored copy.

sections.title: Restore with the TypeScript client
sections.text: Use a private Browser origin and token-file path discovered from its running service. Verify the downloaded file digest against the saved run record before importing. The helper below streams the saved file through the Browser archive API; keep it out of source control.

sections.title: Restore with cURL
sections.text: Use the Browser token, not the Workbench token. POST the raw gzip archive, without a JSON wrapper. The server enforces a 512 MiB import limit. A successful import returns the new profile; inspect it before deleting any original data.

title: Runs and saved results
description: Admit work, inspect state and finish without losing the profile.

sections.title: Choose an installed automation
sections.text: GET /api/v1/automations returns IDs and input schemas. POST /runs with automationId, inputs and optional preset admits one run (HTTP 202). Definitions are installed by the operator; the API does not accept arbitrary script source. Use an Idempotency-Key for recoverable admission and keep input values out of logs. Website effects are not guaranteed exactly once.

sections.title: Observe before controlling
sections.text: GET /runs/{id} reports state, timestamps, cleanup and artifact metadata. Common transitions are queued → starting → running → saving → saved. Runs may pause or await input; cancellation/failure can retain a profile requiring inspection. POST /pause requests a checkpoint pause. Resume continues an eligible paused run; finish completes a script waiting for an explicit operator action. A queued control request is not proof that the browser has stopped.

sections.title: Input and evidence
sections.text: Use the current challengeId and values for /runs/{id}/input. Screenshots and evidence are authenticated and can contain private website content. The events endpoint is SSE notification; durable managed coordinator evidence is a separate stream. Reconcile GET /runs after reconnecting rather than assuming no events were missed.

sections.title: Keep the saved archive
sections.text: When saved, download /runs/{id}/artifact and verify its recorded digest and size. If export failed, retain the original profile, inspect unresolved operations and use retry-export only when eligible. A normal application Quit drains owned work; avoid terminating a live process to force an upgrade.

sections.title: Wait for Ready to finish
sections.text: Open and inspect a browser (inspect) first navigates to your chosen page, then waits for an operator action. Wait until the UI says Ready to finish, or GET /runs/{id} returns waitingForFinish: true, before sending Finish + save or POST /runs/{id}/finish. The running state alone is not sufficient: an early finish returns HTTP 409. Re-read the current run and inspect its state rather than resubmitting the automation.

sections.title: Durable update reconnects
sections.text: GET /api/v1/events sends run notifications with committed journal IDs. Keep the last consumed ID and send Last-Event-ID when reconnecting; the browser EventSource does this automatically. A reset event asks for GET /api/v1/runs because its cursor is new, expired or belongs to another journal. Notification replay never admits or repeats a browser action. Full refreshes preserve newer received updates. History is bounded to 512 notifications and 8 MiB; a write failure closes streams and new streams return 503 until service restart. Run-state reads remain available. Cookie sessions require signing in again after a service restart; bearer clients can resume the retained cursor. Notification commits and canonical run writes are separate transactions, so a notification is not proof that an external action completed.

title: Author and publish flows
description: Keep drafts editable and admitted runs immutable.

sections.title: Draft library
sections.text: GET /api/v1/flow-library returns installed packs, drafts and authoring defaults. POST /flow-library validates a pack, manifest, revision and optional layout. Revision zero creates a draft. Existing writes use the current optimistic revision; a stale update returns HTTP 409. Flow IDs contain 2–64 lowercase letters, digits or hyphens. Use the desktop Flow editor for supported visual controls and review advanced JSON before publication. Saving changed execution content automatically advances the flow patch version above its retained version floor. Unchanged and layout-only saves keep the existing version. The returned pack, hash and revision describe the exact saved definition; use them together. This prevents an edited published flow from colliding with an older admitted version. Flow settings shows the saved version.

sections.title: Branch by recognized page
sections.text: In Flow editor, choose Branch by page. Required states lists the recognized actionable pages this step accepts. Add page route adds a form-controlled destination for another recognized page; remove a route to stop accepting it. The interpreter observes fresh page evidence and chooses that page’s destination without performing a browser action. Unknown or ambiguous pages go through the configured review policy. This is page-state branching, not JavaScript expressions.

sections.title: Repeat a bounded body
sections.text: Choose Repeat steps, set Times to repeat and choose First step in body. Edit body opens its action controls. The body’s last successful route must return to the repeat controller. After repeating sets the destination for each recognized page after the count is exhausted. Counts range from 1 to 99 and also require a step visit limit of at least count + 1, including the final exit. Nested loops count all visits against the same global step, visit and time budgets. Flow settings exposes those limits; Arrange flow places the entry routes before their destinations. Dragging changes layout only. Undo and Redo restore edits before saving.

sections.title: Resume without repeating uncertain effects
sections.text: The journal records each admitted loop iteration and its next step before browser input. After trusted ownership recovery, a controlled flow resumes that saved continuation when fresh page evidence still accepts it. Completed inner-loop counters reset for the next outer iteration. Confirmed successful actions can run again in the next counted iteration; an unresolved or uncertain mutation keeps its existing action fence and cannot silently become a new iteration. A counted iteration is not a guarantee of exactly-once external effects; inspect uncertain outcomes before resuming.

sections.title: Publish the intended revision
sections.text: POST /flow-library/{id}/publish with revision publishes that exact draft. New runs can select the published automation. A run retains its admitted hashed definition even when a later draft is saved or published. Origins and native engine policies still need to satisfy the runtime’s allowlist.

sections.title: Recognize uncertain actions
sections.text: Branches and counted repeats have visual controls. Recognition rules, extraction details and some advanced routes still use their dedicated settings or advanced JSON. An uncertain action is not a successful transition. Inspect evidence and retained profiles before deciding to resume; never force a replay that might repeat a website side effect.

title: Schedules and timezones
description: Preview calendar rules and handle missed or uncertain occurrences.

sections.title: Create the right recurrence
sections.text: POST /api/v1/schedules accepts name, automationId and inputs with nextAt for a one-time schedule, intervalMs for an interval, or cron and optional timezone for a calendar. Do not combine interval and cron. Cron uses five minute-resolution fields; hashed fields are rejected. An optional nextAt is a not-before boundary. Intervals range from one minute to one year.

sections.title: Preview local wall time
sections.text: POST /schedules/preview accepts cron, timezone and optional after (UTC milliseconds), returning the next five UTC occurrence timestamps. Use an IANA name such as Europe/London so calendar wall time follows daylight-saving changes. Preview before creating the schedule.

sections.title: Pause, resume and remove
sections.text: POST /schedules/{id}/pause disables future occurrences. Resume enables an eligible waiting schedule; completed or quarantined schedules require inspection and replacement. Remove deletes the schedule and its vaulted inputs. Inputs are encrypted locally and omitted from public schedule records.

sections.title: Service and recovery limits
sections.text: Workbench must be running; scheduling does not wake a sleeping or powered-off PC. Missed repeating occurrences coalesce into one run rather than bursting. Admission waits for idle capacity and resolved cleanup. A crash during unknown admission quarantines the schedule instead of blindly replaying website actions.

title: Errors and safe recovery
description: Handle conflicts, authentication failures and uncertain operations.

sections.title: Read structured errors
sections.text: Workbench errors return an error message. Browser also returns a code such as unauthorized, conflict or revision_conflict. HTTP 400 indicates invalid input, 401 a missing/invalid token, 403 a disallowed origin or access, 404 a missing resource, 409 a state/lease/admission conflict and 412 a stale Browser revision. HTTP 413 is an upload/body limit and 415 an unsupported content type. Upstream failures may be sanitized.

sections.title: Retry with evidence
sections.text: Re-read the affected resource after a network timeout. Use the same idempotency key only for the identical supported admission request. Do not automatically repeat a non-idempotent website effect. Keep retained profiles, leases, artifacts and failure evidence until recovery is confirmed. Large load, forced-exit and full rollback matrices remain unfinished.

sections.title: Protect the local store
sections.text: Quit through the application before replacing installed files. Upgrade safeguards require idle services and a verified private backup. Never remove a live lease or copy a running database as an assumed valid backup. Documentation does not change profiles, credentials, runs or schedules. Keep private stores, signing keys and vendor binaries out of public repositories.
